title: Debt and ease
hook: pay debts, and be easy on debtors (2:280)
tomorrow: groceries for your own family: a chore, or charity?

segments.voice: Yesterday, paying wages: two readings, one rule, never make the worker chase it. Before the sweat dries. Today, the money that's owed and can't come.
screen: `BEFORE THE SWEAT DRIES.` → `OWED, AND CAN'T COME.`

segments.voice: An index card taped beside a register, a name at the top and a column of numbers in pencil. A folded IOU in a kitchen drawer, gone soft from being opened. The small scratch of a pen when a line gets crossed out. Somebody owes, and they can't pay. Now what? The Qur'an answers in two steps, in Pickthall's words: "And if the debtor is in straitened circumstances, then (let there be) postponement to (the time of) ease".
screen: `A TAB IN PENCIL.` → `AN IOU GONE SOFT.` → `POSTPONEMENT TO EASE.`

segments.voice: Step one is time. If the debtor is struggling, you wait until things ease. Step two comes in the same verse: to let the debt go, as charity, as sadaqah, is better for you, if you only knew. Wait first, and then, if you can, cross the line out. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari tells of a merchant who lent to people and told his servant: when you come to someone in hardship, overlook it, so that perhaps God will overlook us. And the Prophet ﷺ said God overlooked him. The ease he gave came back to him. But the verse isn't a loophole for the one who owes. The same collection has the Prophet calling delay by someone who is able to pay an injustice. So there are two hands in every debt. The borrower's: pay when you can, and don't stall. The lender's: when they truly can't, give them room, and maybe give them the whole of it. One to tell a friend: in that report, a merchant's whole record came down to how he treated people who couldn't pay.
screen: `STEP ONE: TIME.` · `STEP TWO: LET IT GO, AS CHARITY.` · `THE MERCHANT GOD OVERLOOKED.` · `ABLE, AND DELAYING: UNJUST.` · then, large: `EASE FOR THE DEBTOR.`

segments.voice: Hold a coin, or any small thing, in your open palm and feel its weight. Bring to mind one debt, one you owe or one owed to you by someone who's struggling. Close your hand around it for a debt you'll pay; leave it open and flat for one you might ease. Stay with the weight for the rest of the sit.
screen: `A COIN IN YOUR PALM.` · `CLOSED: I'LL PAY.` · `OPEN: I'LL EASE.`

segments.voice: Debt and ease: pay what you owe when you're able, and give the struggling debtor time, or let it go as charity.
Something to keep: ease for the debtor, time first, and maybe the whole of it. The tab can wait.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to repay debts promptly when able, to write debts down, and, as lenders, to give a struggling borrower more time or forgive the debt as charity.
